source_text: In primo enim opere latius disputata sunt. Quamvis nec tu dilucide loquaris, quam mortem intellegi velis, cuius corpus dicis in paradiso non fuisse ante peccatum; quia in libris, quos ad Marcellini nomen edidisti, mortalem Adam factum fuisse professus es [n147] . Quod vero adiungis morbum esse negotium nuptiarum, leniter audiri potest, si hoc solum de tuis parentibus dicas. Conscius enim forte esse potes matris tuae morbi alicuius occulti, quam in libris Confessionis, ut ipso verbo utar, meribibulam vocatam esse signasti [n148] . Ceterum in sanctorum connubio, et in omnium honestorum, nullus omnino morbus est. Quia nec Apostolus morbum pro remedio concessit, cum per reverentiam nuptia m a morbo fornicationis, Ecclesiae homines muniebat; qui sensus quomodo et frontem tuam et dogma penitus eraserit, primi voluminis mei prope ultima parte monstratur; quod et in toto ipsius responsionis corpore, prout locorum opportunitas attulit, explicatum est.
pass_a_gloss: For in the first work they have been disputed more widely. Although neither do you speak clearly, which death you want to be understood, whose body you say was not in paradise before sin; because in the books which you published to the name of Marcellinus, you professed that Adam had been made mortal. But what you join, that the business of marriages is a disease, can be heard gently, if you say this only about your own parents. For perhaps you can be conscious of some hidden disease of your mother, whom in the books of the Confession, that I may use the very word, you marked to have been called a wine-bibber. For the rest in the marriage of the saints, and in that of all honorable people, there is no disease at all. Because neither did the Apostle concede a disease for a remedy, when through reverence of marriage he was fortifying the humans of the Church from the disease of fornication; which sense, how it has thoroughly erased both your forehead and your dogma, is shown in nearly the last part of my first volume; which also in the whole body of that answer itself, as the opportuneness of places brought, has been unfolded.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS nuptiae=nuptials; Blaise Christian marriage good

pass_b_english: These matters were discussed at greater length in my first work. Yet you do not speak clearly about which death you mean when you say that its body did not exist in paradise before sin, since in the books published under Marcellinus's name you acknowledged that Adam was made mortal (Augustine, On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins 1.3–4). As for your addition that the business of marriage is a disease, that can be heard calmly if you say it only about your own parents. Perhaps you know of some hidden disease of your mother's, whom you recorded in the Confessions as having been called, to use the very word, a wine-tippler (Augustine, Confessions 9.18). But in the marriages of the saints and of all honorable people there is no disease whatsoever. Nor did the apostle allow a disease as a remedy when, through respect for marriage, he protected the people of the Church from the disease of fornication (compare 1 Corinthians 7:2). Near the end of my first book I show how completely that meaning wipes out both your effrontery and your doctrine. I also explained it throughout the whole body of that reply as the occasion arose (1 Corinthians 7:2).

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
Julian defends marriage as God's work against the charge that generation transmits sin.
